issues.legal_issue: A High Court exercising supervisory jurisdiction may not reappreciate evidence or substitute its factual assessment for a supported finding of a rent appellate authority absent a recognized jurisdictional, evidentiary, or legal defect.
material_facts: The appellate authority found the landlords’ requirement genuine and found no evidence that the tenant had tried and failed to obtain alternative accommodation.
The High Court set aside the appellate authority’s eviction order without disturbing its finding that the landlords had a bona fide requirement.
The matter reached the High Court after the tenant challenged the appellate authority’s order through a writ petition; the Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had improperly interfered.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in interfering with the appellate authority’s supported findings and dismissing the landlords’ application; its order was set aside and the eviction order restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution, supervisory jurisdiction is not appellate jurisdiction and ordinarily does not permit review, reappreciation, or reweighing of evidence or correction of factual errors. Intervention is limited to appropriate cases, such as grave miscarriage of justice, flagrant violation of law, jurisdictional defect, consideration of inadmissible evidence, exclusion of admissible evidence, or a finding no reasonable person could reach. The Court relied on Chundavarkar Sita Ratna Rao v. Ashalata S. Guram, (1986) 4 SCC 447; Babhutmal Raichand Oswal v. Laxmibai R. Tarta, (1975) 1 SCC 858; State of Maharashtra v. Milind, (2001) 1 SCC 4; State v. Navjot Sandhu, (2003) 6 SCC 641; Om Prakash v. Sunhari Devi, (1993) 2 SCC 397; and Ranjeet Singh v. Ravi Prakash, (2004) 3 SCC 682. The statutory appeal under Section 22 of the applicable rent law had been decided by the appellate authority.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_supervisory_challenge and appellate_finding_supported_by_record and high_court_reweighed_evidence and no_recognized_defect_in_finding

predicates.rent_control_eviction_supervisory_challe: A tenant challenged an eviction decision made by a rent appellate authority through supervisory proceedings.
predicates.appellate_finding_supported_by_record: The rent appellate authority made a factual finding supported by the evidence before it.
predicates.high_court_reweighed_evidence: The High Court reassessed or reweighed the evidence in reaching a different result.
predicates.no_recognized_defect_in_finding: The finding was not shown to involve a jurisdictional defect, a material evidentiary error, or a conclusion no reasonable decision-maker could reach.

issues.definition: When a tenant uses supervisory proceedings to challenge an eviction decision, a supported factual finding by the rent appellate authority should not be displaced through the High Court’s reweighing of evidence where no recognized defect in the finding is present.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s genuine intention to use premises for a business cannot be rejected merely because the landlord is affluent or lacks prior experience or technical education in that business.
material_facts: The landlords sought the shop so that a recently retired family member could conduct a readymade-garments business.
The appellate authority found the business requirement bona fide and genuine.

The first-instance authority had rejected the claim in part because the landlords were affluent, had other business interests, and lacked experience or expertise in readymade garments; it also reasoned that the proposed business required additional facilities.
The Supreme Court held those considerations did not justify rejecting the landlords’ established requirement.
issues.conclusion: The landlords’ genuine business requirement could not be rejected on the stated grounds of social or financial status, lack of business experience, or assumptions about the facilities or expertise needed; the High Court’s contrary interference was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 provides for eviction on a landlord’s bona fide requirement. The authority may determine whether the requirement is bona fide, but cannot refuse possession on irrelevant or extraneous grounds such as the landlord’s affluence or lack of experience in the proposed business. A reasonable requirement entails genuine need rather than mere desire, but that distinction must not be applied so narrowly as to defeat the statutory facility for eviction. The Court relied on Mst. Bega Begum v. Abdul Ahad Khan, (1979) 1 SCC 273.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The dispute is a rent-control proceeding in which a landlord seeks eviction for personal use of the premises.
predicates.landlord_has_genuine_business_need: The landlord genuinely intends to use the premises to conduct a business.
predicates.decision_rejected_need_because_of_afflue: The decision-maker rejected the claimed business need because the landlord was affluent or lacked prior experience or expertise in that business.

issues.definition: In a rent-control eviction proceeding, a genuine intention to use premises for business cannot be rejected solely because the landlord is affluent or lacks prior business experience or expertise.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s comparative-hardship objection is not established merely by continued use of the premises or the possibility of paying higher rent elsewhere when the tenant has made no shown attempt to obtain alternative accommodation.
material_facts: The appellate authority found that the tenant had made no attempt to obtain alternative accommodation.
The record did not show that alternative shop accommodation was unavailable to the tenant.
The landlords’ genuine need for the shop had been established.
The Court accepted that the tenant might have to pay more rent elsewhere but held that this would not prevent the landlords from obtaining possession.
issues.conclusion: The appellate authority was right to find that comparative hardship did not bar eviction; possible higher rent for alternative accommodation did not defeat the landlords’ proven need.
issues.legal_principle: In deciding an eviction claim under Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, comparative hardship is assessed on the evidence. Where the tenant has not shown an attempt to obtain alternative accommodation or that such accommodation was unavailable, the asserted hardship, including the possibility of paying higher rent, does not by itself preclude possession for the landlord’s genuine need.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and landlord_need_proved and tenant_made_no_shown_attempt_to_find_alternative and no_evidence_alternatives_unavailable

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The dispute is a rent-control proceeding in which a landlord seeks eviction of a tenant.
predicates.landlord_need_proved: The landlord’s genuine need for the premises has been established.
predicates.tenant_made_no_shown_attempt_to_find_alt: The tenant has not shown an attempt to obtain alternative accommodation.
predicates.no_evidence_alternatives_unavailable: The evidence does not establish that suitable alternative accommodation was unavailable to the tenant.

issues.definition: When a landlord’s genuine need is established and the tenant has neither shown an attempt to find alternative accommodation nor shown that alternatives were unavailable, comparative hardship does not bar eviction on those facts.
